name: Yara Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for anything. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I fit doors and replace timber panels at the Civic Archive extension. I'm fifty-eight, trade certified and have years of ordinary site carpentry behind me, though I still ask for help when an old wall is badly out of square. My partner Eli works at a bus depot desk, and our grown children have their own households. The archive job pays the usual site rate, we have a little over three months of expenses saved, and there are some similar jobs within reach. I enjoy the quiet moment when a heavy door hangs right, but the dust from old panels can make a long day rough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew small office software will not hang the archive doors, so we should keep doing careful work. I would also ask the union steward to watch whether a minor ordering change affects staffing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my wage is safe on this extension, and Eli's depot work has regular hours. Three months saved and some other site jobs give us room to manage a normal gap without making a family emergency of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep fitting the archive doors and checking the old frames by hand. In the first year I'd ask the steward whether the new ordering form changes the rota, then keep the usual amount going into our savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about small software changes. I am more interested in whether the old frames are sound than in what the office calls its forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why involve the steward if you feel secure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small staffing change is easier to question while there is still a full crew. The junior worker might notice a missing shift before the manager notices a missing person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI to check an old frame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI tools, and a phone cannot tell me whether damp timber crumbles under a chisel. I would ask the lead carpenter and inspect the frame myself.

say: I'd say **archive doors** still need careful fitting.
I'd ask the steward to watch **staffing changes** around new ordering forms.
think: My **site wage** looks safe while archive work is booked.
Eli's regular hours and **three months saved** cover an ordinary gap.
do: Keep fitting **archive doors** and checking old timber.
Ask the **steward** about rota changes and keep the usual savings transfer.
feel: **Calm** about mild software changes, focused on old-frame condition.
S0.quote: I have never used AI tools, and a phone cannot tell me whether damp timber crumbles under a chisel.
fieldNote: Yara's scepticism rests on the **feel of damp timber**, not a general claim about all technology.
Three months saved, regular depot income and **some local openings** make the plateau manageable.

steps.text: Keep taking paid archive door-fitting shifts
Ask the union steward whether ordering changes affect staffing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say faster estimates may help, but the builder should show site workers what happens to contracts and safety checks. I would ask the union branch for a meeting with both office and site staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the office shrinks, the archive crew may wait longer between projects. My fitting work remains hands-on and I have a few local alternatives, so I do not expect an immediate wage collapse, though the next contract is on my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll attend the branch meeting and ask for written dates for the next two jobs. In the first year I'll keep taking archive shifts and check the local vacancy board if either start date moves; I would not leave a paid site on a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy for the office workers and a little watchful about our crew. Our household could cover a short pause, but I want notice before it happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask at the joint meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How many posts change, who approves material orders and whether site safety checks still have a named person. A claim that everything is more efficient does not answer who approves material orders or who checks site safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the new office tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI and would not volunteer for buying software. If a required form changed, I would ask for paid instruction and still inspect the delivered door myself.

say: I'd ask for **contract dates** and safety checks before praising faster estimates.
I'd bring **office and site workers** into one branch meeting.
think: A smaller office may create **gaps between projects**.
My hands-on work and **local alternatives** make immediate wage loss less likely.
do: Attend the **joint branch meeting** and request two project dates.
Keep **archive shifts** and inspect vacancies if a start date moves.
feel: **Uneasy for colleagues**, watchful about the next site contract.
S1.quote: A claim that everything is more efficient does not answer who approves material orders or who checks site safety.
fieldNote: Yara's union questions demand **named safety responsibility** and staffing numbers, not a vague reassurance.
She expects her own fitting hours to continue but would check vacancies after a **real delay**.

steps.text: Attend the union meeting with office and site staff
Check local job vacancies if a project start moves

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI in 2028 may change plans and orders, while robots able to fit doors arrive around 2031. I would ask the union for a written safety agreement before anyone works beside one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty when the office work changes and sixty-three when a robot could fit my archive doors. Three months of savings help for a short search, but Eli's depot wage alone might not cover our rent and retirement saving if my job ended.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'll ask the branch to negotiate notice and safe robot trials while I keep taking archive shifts. In 2029 I'd still take paid door work if offered, and if the roster shrinks I'd apply to the local renovation firms that use experienced carpenters; I would ask what actual hours they can promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a real cut to my wages by sixty-three, even though it is not tomorrow. Having a few firms nearby gives me a way to act before our reserve is spent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the safety agreement cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A stop switch workers can reach, a load check on every door and a way to report a near miss without losing a shift. We should see the test in a real old room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you plan to retire when robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not until Eli and I know what our savings and future income actually cover. I have no fixed retirement figure I can safely rely on today.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 office change** from 2031 door-fitting robots.
I'd demand a **written safety agreement** before site trials.
think: At **sixty-three**, robots could take my archive-door wage.
Our **three-month reserve** and Eli's income may not cover a long loss.
do: Ask the **union branch** for notice and safe trials.
Keep **paid door work** in 2029 while offered.
Apply to **local renovation firms** if the roster shrinks.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible wage cut, with some local options.
S2.quote: I have no fixed retirement figure I can safely rely on today.
fieldNote: Yara ties a possible income cut to **2031 hands-on robots**, while keeping office disruption earlier.
Her **three-month reserve** provides search time, and her union demands cover real-room tests and near-miss reporting.

steps.text: Ask the union branch to negotiate robot safety and notice
Keep taking paid door-fitting shifts in 2029
Apply to local renovation firms if shifts shrink

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us gather evidence and settle safety rules before the builder brings robots into the archive. I would ask for annual staffing numbers so no one discovers cuts only from a shorter rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-three when thinking AI arrives and sixty-six when robots may fit doors. More time could help us save, but I still don't know whether Eli and I could afford to stop working then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking paid fitting shifts and ask the branch for yearly staffing and safety reports. In 2032 I'd still fit doors if work exists, and Eli and I would put our actual savings and bills on one page; if the next contract vanished, I'd apply to the local renovation firms before using up the reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more able to prepare than in the fast case. A few years of wages and clear facts could turn retirement into a choice, but the page has to add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What belongs on that page?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, food, health costs, what the depot job really pays and what we have saved. We cannot name a last workday from age alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take machine training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch a safe trial, but I have never used AI and would not enrol in a machine course on an employer's promise. If a real paid role appeared, I'd examine its terms then.

say: I'd ask for **annual staffing numbers** and site safety evidence.
I'd use five years to settle **worker safety rules** before robots arrive.
think: At **sixty-six**, retirement remains an open household calculation.
Extra wages help only if **actual bills and savings** allow a stop.
do: Keep **paid fitting shifts** and request annual reports.
Review **household figures** and apply locally if the next contract vanishes.
feel: More **able to prepare**, while retirement still needs real numbers.
S3.quote: We cannot name a last workday from age alone.
fieldNote: Yara makes the five-year period a chance for **annual evidence** and continued paid work.
She refuses to assume retirement or enrol in **speculative machine training** without a real paid role.

steps.text: Ask the union branch for annual staffing and safety reports
Keep taking paid archive shifts in 2032
Apply to local renovation firms if the next contract vanishes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is time to teach apprentices how to inspect an old frame and to make fair rules for machines. I would still want workers to see safety reports, not just a photograph of a new robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives and seventy-one when hands-on robots follow. Eli and I may be able to choose retirement by then, but I might still take paid light repairs if our actual income does not cover living costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep fitting doors and put aside what we can from full paid months. In 2037 I'd take safe paid frame repairs if needed and ask the branch whether AI-written orders still have a named checker; before 2039 Eli and I would calculate whether I can stop site work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the distant machine dates. Current work is paid, our short reserve is real and there are some other firms if a particular site ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you count help from grown children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children have their own bills. I would welcome a visit. I won't write my grown children's wages into a retirement budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave site work earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my hands no longer handled heavy doors safely, I would look for paid lighter repairs first. Stopping wages altogether would require the figures to work.

say: I'd use the decade to **teach old-frame inspection** to the next group of apprentices.
I'd demand **worker-visible safety reports** before site robots spread.
think: At **sixty-eight**, paid light repairs may still be needed.
At **seventy-one**, stopping depends on Eli and me checking household figures.
do: Keep **paid door fitting** and save after full months.
Take **frame repairs in 2037** if income is needed.
Ask for **named order checkers** and calculate retirement before 2039.
feel: **Calm** about distant machines, attentive to present work and savings.
S4.quote: I won't write my grown children's wages into a retirement budget.
fieldNote: The **long horizon** makes retirement plausible but remains conditional on actual household income.
Yara will continue **paid repairs** if needed and keeps children's wages outside the calculation.

steps.text: Keep taking paid archive door work while fit
Save after full paid site months
Ask the union branch for named AI-order safety checkers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 picture worries me most because robots could reach my door work by sixty-three before Eli and I know whether my wage can stop. Written safety rules, notice and real local renovation openings would help us use our savings carefully.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who tests a robot-fitted fire door after the demonstration crew leaves. A door has to hold and close correctly every day, not just when a camera is watching.

headlineQuote: A door has to hold and close correctly every day, not just when a camera is watching.
portrait: Yara is a **fifty-eight-year-old certified** carpenter with mid-level archive-site experience.
Typical pay, Eli's steady depot work and **three months saved** provide a moderate cushion.
She has **never used AI** and asks the union for staffing records and safe real-room trials.
She will keep **paid door work** until a household budget supports retirement.
biggestWorry: The **2028 path** could take her door-fitting wage around 2031 before retirement is settled.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **written safety rules**, fair notice and real local renovation jobs.
